justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—612.17 in this case—are primarily driven by the central tendency of the data available at the time of the forecast. This likely reflects the most probable trajectory based on historical trends, underlying patterns in the data, or whatever key predictive model was employed. Essentially, the point estimate represents the "best guess," assuming normal conditions persist and that no significant disruptions or unexpected events occur. Consistency in the point estimate across all horizons reflects an expectation of stability or a baseline assumption that the underlying factors influencing the data are unlikely to change drastically over the short term.

The width of the confidence intervals reflects the degree of uncertainty associated with the forecast, and it naturally grows as you extend the time horizon. For the 1-day forecast, the confidence interval is relatively narrow (606.05 to 618.29) because the short time frame minimizes the chances of unexpected deviations. By contrast, the 1-week and 1-month forecast intervals are significantly wider, reflecting additional sources of uncertainty that accumulate over longer periods. These uncertainties could include volatile market conditions, shifts in external factors, or simply the natural variability in the system being modeled. Over a month, for instance, the confidence interval expands the most (from 550.0 to 674.34) because it has to account for a broader range of possible scenarios, including compounding errors and unforeseen influences.

Outside of these intervals, specific risks or events could cause outcomes to deviate more dramatically. For example, abrupt, highly impactful events like geopolitical turmoil, significant policy changes, or unexpected economic shocks could disrupt the normal patterns the forecast is based on. Similarly, idiosyncratic risks tied to the system or entity being modeled could create large, unpredictable swings. While these events are difficult to predict in terms of timing and magnitude, they are part of the reason why confidence intervals exist—to represent a range of plausible outcomes—but extreme disruptions (sometimes referred to as "tail risks") can still push outcomes outside even well-thought-out predictions.
